phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) dental stop [dʲ], the tongue raised toward the hard palate — the soft 'dy' onset Irish keeps to this day.
Short front [e] followed by a slender r [ɾʲ], the stressed syllable — brief and bright, never the English 'eer'.
Lenited [ð], the voiced dental fricative of English 'this', running into a second slender r [ɾʲ]; the manuscript writes plain d, the sound has softened.
The close front ending [u] with a palatal off-glide — the Old Irish nominative Derdriu ends on a light rising note.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DYER-dryu' — stress the first syllable; slender d, short 'e', the second d melted into the soft 'th' of 'this'. Modern Irish says 'DYER-dra', and English has long settled on 'DEER-dree'.

pronunciation.note: Deirdre is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the standing of Ireland's most tragic heroine in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Tragedy, Beauty
domains.subtitle: The Woman the Prophecy Named, Ireland's Most Sorrowful Heroine
domains.lead: Deirdre is the tragic heart of the Ulster Cycle: the girl whose beauty a druid prophesied at birth would bring ruin on Ulster, raised in secret by King Conchobar mac Nessa to be his own bride, who chose instead the young Naoise son of Uisnech and fled with him and his brothers to Alba. Lured home by a king's treachery, she saw her lovers slain at Emain Macha, lived a year without smiling, and dashed out her own life rather than pass to the man who had betrayed her — the death that made her, in the medieval phrase, the heroine of one of the Three Sorrowful Tales of Ireland.

cards.name: The Raven on the Snow
cards.desc: She saw a raven drinking blood in the snow and wished for a man with hair black as the raven, cheeks red as the blood, skin white as the snow — and Lebarcham named Naoise.

cards.name: The Sons of Uisnech
cards.desc: Naoise, Ardan, and Ainnle — the three brothers whose singing could lull the world, whose exile and death the whole tale turns upon.

cards.name: Emain Macha
cards.desc: Conchobar's royal seat, the court that raised her, the fort where the sons of Uisnech were slain — and the place she would not survive.

cards.name: The Two Trees
cards.desc: In the later telling, two yews grew from the graves of Deirdre and Naoise and wove their tops together over Emain Macha — love outlasting the king.

symbols.name: The raven, the blood, the snow
symbols.meaning: The three colours of her desire, spoken before she had seen a man — the wish the whole tragedy answers

symbols.name: The three sons of Uisnech
symbols.meaning: Naoise, Ardan, and Ainnle — one fate shared by three brothers; loyalty that follows her into exile and death

symbols.name: Emain Macha
symbols.meaning: The royal fort of Ulster — safety that was a cage, and the gate to which exile could not safely return

symbols.name: The crossing to Alba
symbols.meaning: The sea between Ireland and Scotland — the only escape the tale allows, and never a lasting one

symbols.name: The two entwined trees
symbols.meaning: Yews from the lovers' graves woven together — the later tradition's one gesture toward consolation

mythology.lead: Deirdre's story is the most perfectly shaped tragedy in medieval Irish literature: a prophecy, a wish, an elopement, an exile, a betrayal, and a death, told in Longes mac nUislenn — the Exile of the Sons of Uisnech — with an economy no retelling has improved. It is a fore-tale of the Táin, and it leaves Ulster's honour in ruins before the great cattle-raid ever begins.

myths.title: The Prophecy at Her Birth
myths.text:
She was born to trouble. At the feast of Fedlimid mac Daill, Conchobar's storyteller, Fedlimid's wife cried out from the womb she carried, and the druid Cathbad laid his hand on her belly and spoke the child's fate: a girl of yellow hair and grey eyes and foxglove lips, whose beauty would be ruin — kings would fight for her, the sons of Uisnech would die for her, and Ulster would lose its greatest heroes because of her. The warriors of Ulster cried out to kill the infant at once.

Conchobar refused. He would take the child, he said, and raise her apart, and she would be his own wife — no one else's ruin. So Deirdre was reared in a secluded house with her foster-parents and her nurse Lebarcham, seeing no man but those three and the king who meant to claim her. The prophecy is the tale's first sentence; everything after is its unfolding.

myths.title: The Raven on the Snow
myths.text:
One winter day her foster-father flayed a calf in the snow for her dinner, and a raven came down to drink the blood. Deirdre looked at the three colours and said to Lebarcham: she could love a man with those three colours — hair black as the raven, cheeks red as the blood, skin white as the snow. Lebarcham told her such a man was near: Naoise son of Uisnech, of Conchobar's own household.

Deirdre sent for him, and when Naoise came she put her two hands on his ears — 'two ears of shame and derision,' she said, if he would not take her away — and bound him by the honour of an Ulster warrior. That night Naoise took her, and with his brothers Ardan and Ainnle and a hundred and fifty warriors they fled the king's house. The wish spoken over the calf's blood is the tale's hinge: the one moment Deirdre chooses, and all the rest follows from the choosing.

myths.title: The Exile in Alba
myths.text:
Conchobar pursued them through Ireland until they crossed the sea to Alba, and there they made a life the tale calls happy: the sons of Uisnech hunted, Deirdre kept house, and their singing was famous. But the same pattern waited across the water — the king of Alba heard of her beauty and desired her, and the brothers had to fight free and flee again, from glen to glen and island to island, until no place in Alba was safe for a woman too beautiful and the men who would not give her up.

It was then that Conchobar's messengers came with peace on their lips. The king swore he longed for them; he sent sureties — in the old version, Fergus mac Róich, Conchobar's greatest champion, stood pledge for their safety. Deirdre alone did not believe it. She had dreamed, she said, of three birds from Emain carrying honey in their beaks who left with blood — the honey the fair words, the blood the truth of them. But the sons of Uisnech trusted the surety of Fergus, and they sailed home.

myths.tag: Longes mac nUislenn / Oided mac nUislenn
myths.title: The Betrayal at Emain Macha
myths.text:
The trap was laid in the old way, through honour itself. As Fergus escorted the exiles south he was detained by an engineered feast — a geis-bound invitation he could not refuse — and sent the sons of Uisnech on to Emain under the protection of his sons, while Deirdre sang warnings at every stop. At Emain they were lodged in the house of the Red Branch, and when Conchobar sent to know whether Deirdre had kept her looks, and heard she had, he sent his warrior Maine against the house. The sons of Uisnech fought; the sons of Fergus died defending them; and at last Naoise and Ardan and Ainnle were cut down together, one sword-stroke taking the three, as Deirdre had foreseen in the blood-red dream.

Then Deirdre sang the laments the tradition kept as the summit of Irish elegy — for Naoise, 'fair and great and gentle', for the brothers, for the dún they would see no more. The betrayal broke Ulster: Fergus and three thousand of the Ulaid went into exile to Connacht, to Ailill and Medb — and that is why, when the Táin begins, Ulster's greatest champion stands in the enemy's host. Deirdre's tragedy is the Táin's hidden prologue.

myths.title: The Year Without a Smile, and the Death
myths.text:
Conchobar took Deirdre, and for a year she lived in his house and did not smile, did not raise her head from her knee, did not eat her fill or sleep her fill. When the king asked what she hated most in the world, she answered: 'You, and Éogan mac Durthacht' — the man who had struck down Naoise. So Conchobar gave her to Éogan, to be passed like a debt between the two men she loathed.

The next day she was driven beside Éogan's chariot, and as they went she saw the standing stone before her and put her head out of the chariot and dashed it against the rock, and so died. The later telling, Oided mac nUislenn, gives the tradition its consolation: she was buried beside Naoise, a yew grew from each grave, and the two trees wove their tops together over Emain Macha. The old version grants no such mercy — it ends with a woman who had been a prize since the hour of her birth taking back, in the only way left, the disposal of herself.

lore.syncretism: The Welsh corpus knows no Deirdre, and the silence is honest: the Mabinogi and its wider tradition preserve no figure derived from her name. The instructive comparison within Celtic literature is structural — Blodeuwedd in the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, the woman made from flowers for a husband she does not choose, who takes her own lover and pays for it: the medieval Celtic literatures staged, more than once, the tragedy of a woman treated as a thing made or kept for a man. Scholars have also compared the wider motif-cluster — the beauty prophesied at birth to ruin a kingdom — with the classical pattern of Helen, a comparison of motifs, never of descent. Within Ireland, her closest company is the cycle's own doomed: the tradition itself grouped her tale with the Children of Lir and the sons of Tuireann as the Three Sorrowful Tales of Ireland, and her one year of silence beside Conchobar is the cycle's starkest answer to a king's power.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Irish heroine has had a longer afterlife. The Gaelic tradition of Scotland kept her in Alba — the late recension of her death-tale survives in the Glenmasan manuscript, and Argyll named her exile's glens and lochs after her. The Irish literary revival made her its central woman: AE staged Deirdre in 1902, Yeats his Deirdre in 1907, Lady Gregory wove the tale through Cuchulain of Muirthemne, and J. M. Synge left at his death the unfinished Deirdre of the Sorrows (1910), the play that fixed her English name — the sorrows — forever. In the revolutionary generation she became an emblem of Ireland itself, the beautiful land betrayed and bereaved; and the name never left the language, Deirdre remaining a living Irish given name into the present century.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Deirdre is the rare tragic heroine whose tragedy is not what she suffers but what she is denied: a single choice. The tale gives her exactly one free act — the wish by the calf's blood, the hands on Naoise's ears — and then spends its length closing every door it opened. The druid's prophecy is not a curse on her; it is a verdict on everyone around her, and the tale is careful to prove the druid right by the men's deeds, not hers. Conchobar's 'mercy' at her birth is only a longer leash; Fergus's surety is only a prettier trap. What the sons of Uisnech die of is not her beauty but a king's appetite wearing the mask of pardon.

Her answer, when every door is shut, is the hardest the Irish corpus knows: a year of silence, and then the standing stone. The medieval tale does not sentimentalize it. She will not be consoled, will not smile, will not be passed on; the later tradition added the entwined yews because the audience needed the mercy, but the old text ends at the rock. Ireland grouped her story among its Three Sorrowful Tales not because a woman died, but because a whole kingdom's honour died with her — and the woman, in the end, was the only one who kept hers.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in the Book of Leinster in the Old Irish form Derdriu, written in the Insular Latin script — plain Latin letters, with no diacritic for the restoration to recover; the temple form Deirdre is the normalized Modern Irish spelling. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: deirdre.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Deirdre is a textual heroine: no ogham stone names her and no votive inscription invokes her, as befits a figure of heroic legend rather than cult. Her mythic address, however, is one of the most excavated sites in Ireland: Emain Macha, Conchobar's royal seat, survives as Navan Fort in County Armagh, where excavation revealed a great circular timber structure of the first century BC — raised, filled with stones, burned, and mounded over in what reads as a single enormous ritual act, dated by dendrochronology to 95/94 BC. Her manuscript witnesses are exact: Longes mac nUislenn survives earliest in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster (Trinity College Dublin, MS H 2.18), the basis of Hull's edition, while the expanded death-tale Oided mac nUislenn is preserved in the fifteenth-century Glenmasan manuscript (National Library of Scotland, Advocates' MS 72.1.37), the text that carried her story into the Gaelic tradition of Scotland. The name itself was a real one: eDIL records Derdriu as an ordinary woman's name in early Irish sources, so the heroine bore a name of her own world, not an invented one.
